3	from markdown_it import MarkdownIt
4	from markdown_it.tree import SyntaxTreeNode
5	
6	_LIST_ITEM = re.compile(r"^\s*([-*+]|\d+\.)\s+")
7	_FENCE = re.compile(r"^[ ]{0,3}(```|~~~)")
8	_TABLE_ROW = re.compile(r"^\s*\|.*\|\s*$")
9	_HEADING = re.compile(r"^\s*#{1,6}\s+")
10	
11	_TAG_SHAPE = r"</?([A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*(?:\s[^<>]*?)?)\s*/?>"
12	_SPOKEN_HTML_TAG = re.compile(rf"\\?{_TAG_SHAPE}")
13	
14	_md = MarkdownIt("commonmark").enable("table")
15	
16	_ORDINALS = [
17	    "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten",
18	    "Eleven", "Twelve", "Thirteen", "Fourteen", "Fifteen", "Sixteen", "Seventeen",
19	    "Eighteen", "Nineteen", "Twenty",
20	]
21	
22	
23	def is_cruft(text: str, title_norm: str) -> bool:
24	    core = _LIST_ITEM.sub("", _HEADING.sub("", text)).strip()
25	
26	    if title_norm and core.lower() == title_norm:
27	        return True
28	
29	    return is_unspeakable(core)
30	
31	
32	def to_spoken(unit: str, list_mode: str = "current") -> str:
33	    """Render one markdown unit to clean spoken text. list_mode "current" reads a whole
34	    list (however many items) as one run-on sentence, same as every other unit. list_mode
35	    "items" splits it: each top-level and nested item becomes its own sentence, in document
36	    order, an ordered item's sentence prefixed with its spoken number ("One. ...")."""
37	    if _FENCE.match(unit):
38	        return "Code sample."
39	
40	    if _TABLE_ROW.match(unit.lstrip().split("\n", 1)[0]):
41	        return _table_to_spoken(unit)
42	
43	    if list_mode == "items" and _is_list(unit):
44	        return _list_to_spoken_items(unit)
45	
46	    out: list[str] = []
47	
48	    for tok in _md.parse(unit):
49	        if tok.type != "inline":
50	            continue
51	
52	        for child in tok.children or []:
53	            if child.type in ("text", "code_inline"):
54	                out.append(child.content)
55	            elif child.type in ("softbreak", "hardbreak"):
56	                out.append(" ")
57	
58	    return sanitize_spoken("".join(out))
59	
60	
61	def _is_list(unit: str) -> bool:
62	    for line in unit.split("\n"):
63	        stripped = line.strip()
64	        if stripped == "":
65	            continue
66	        return bool(_LIST_ITEM.match(line))
67	    return False
68	
69	
70	def _list_to_spoken_items(unit: str) -> str:
71	    """Walk the parsed tree for one list unit and emit one sentence per list item, an
72	    item's own text flushed before its nested sub-list is walked (so the item that
73	    introduces a nested list reads before its children, not after), an ordered item's
74	    sentence prefixed with its spoken position ("One.") or its literal number past
75	    twenty. A multi-paragraph item's paragraphs are joined into that one sentence."""
76	    tree = SyntaxTreeNode(_md.parse(unit))
77	    sentences: list[str] = []
78	
79	    def collect_own_text(node, parts: list[str]) -> None:
80	        if node.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
81	            return
82	        if node.type == "inline":
83	            for child in node.children:
84	                if child.type in ("text", "code_inline"):
85	                    parts.append(child.content)
86	                elif child.type in ("softbreak", "hardbreak"):
87	                    parts.append(" ")
88	            return
89	        for child in node.children:
90	            collect_own_text(child, parts)
91	
92	    def walk(list_node) -> None:
93	        ordered = list_node.type == "ordered_list"
94	        number = int(list_node.attrs.get("start", 1)) if ordered else 0
95	        for item in list_node.children:
96	            parts: list[str] = []
97	            collect_own_text(item, parts)
98	            text = sanitize_spoken("".join(parts)).rstrip(".")
99	            if text != "":
100	                if ordered:
101	                    prefix = _ORDINALS[number - 1] if 1 <= number <= len(_ORDINALS) else str(number)
102	                    sentences.append(f"{prefix}. {text}.")
103	                else:
104	                    sentences.append(f"{text}.")
105	            if ordered:
106	                number += 1
107	            for child in item.children:
108	                if child.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
109	                    walk(child)
110	
111	    for top in tree.children:
112	        if top.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
113	            walk(top)
114	
115	    return " ".join(sentences)
116	
117	
118	def is_unspeakable(spoken: str) -> bool:
119	    return not any(c.isalnum() for c in spoken)
120	
121	
122	def sanitize_spoken(text: str) -> str:
123	    text = _SPOKEN_HTML_TAG.sub(r"\1", text)
124	    text = re.sub(r"\*\*|__|\*|`", " ", text)
125	    text = re.sub(r"\s+([,.;:!?])", r"\1", text)
126	
127	    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
128	
129	
130	def _table_to_spoken(table: str) -> str:
131	    rows: list[list[str]] = []
132	    cur: list[str] = []
133	
134	    for tok in _md.parse(table):
135	        if tok.type == "inline":
136	            cur.append(tok.content)
137	        elif tok.type == "tr_close":

149	        )

155	    alt = alt.strip()
156	    return f"Image: {alt}." if alt else "Image with no description."

158

160	    return "Code sample."

import argparse
import json
import sys

from to_spoken import code_to_spoken, image_to_spoken, is_unspeakable, to_spoken


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--units", required=True, help="path to the runner's units JSON")
    parser.add_argument("--list-mode", choices=["current", "items"], default="current")
    parser.add_argument("--out", help="path to write the spoken-annotated JSON")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(args.units, "r") as f:
        payload = json.load(f)

    units = payload["units"] if "units" in payload else payload

    results = []
    for unit in units:
        if unit["type"] == "image":
            spoken = image_to_spoken(unit.get("alt", ""))
        elif unit["type"] == "code":
            spoken = code_to_spoken()
        else:
            spoken = to_spoken(unit["display"], list_mode=args.list_mode)

        dropped = is_unspeakable(spoken)
        results.append({**unit, "spoken": spoken, "dropped": dropped})

    if args.out:
        with open(args.out, "w") as f:
            json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
    else:
        json.dump(results, sys.stdout, indent=2)
        print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

1	export const RECIPE_CONTRACT = `
2	A recipe is one JavaScript ES module that imports nothing and exports, by name:
3	
4	- container: a selector string naming the element that holds the article; everything outside it is site chrome.
5	- ignores: a list of { selector, reason } for elements deliberately excluded (ads, date stamps, share rows). Every recipe excludes footnote markers and footnote bodies: declare them here.
6	- inventory: a list of { selector, role } naming every element kind the container carries, role being one of unit (becomes an extracted unit), inline (content inside a unit), wrapper (structural container carrying no content of its own), or title.
7	- extract($, toMarkdown): builds the article from the parsed document.
8	  - $ is a Cheerio document of the article. Read it without changing it; prepare clones instead.
9	  - toMarkdown(element) converts an element to markdown with the fixed converter; every paragraph and code unit's display comes from it.
10	  - It returns { title, units } where each unit is one of:
11	    { type: "paragraph", display, element }
12	    { type: "code", display, element }
13	    { type: "image", src, alt, element }
14	  - Units come back in document order, one element per unit, never overlapping.
15	  - An image the article carries is always emitted, even when its src cannot be resolved; alt is exactly what the page presents and is never invented.
16	
17	Structural preparation (building a thead for a bare table, swapping MathML for its alttext LaTeX, wrapping a span-built listing in a pre, removing footnote subtrees) happens on a cloned element you then pass to toMarkdown.
18	`;
19	
20	export const REPLY_CONTRACT = `
21	The extract tool's recipe argument is the module source itself, never this envelope: the json below belongs only to your final reply.
22	
23	Your final reply is one fenced json block and nothing else after it:
24	
25	- a settled script: \`{"kind": "script", "source": "<the full recipe module source>"}\`
26	- the page is not an article: \`{"kind": "not-article"}\`
27	- you give up: \`{"kind": "gave-up", "reason": "<why>"}\`
28	
29	Never include the extracted units in the reply: the recipe itself is re-run deterministically to produce them.
30	`;
31	
32	function articleSection(html: string): string {
33	  return `The article's html:
34	
35	\`\`\`html
36	${html}
37	\`\`\``;
38	}
39	
40	export function authorInstruction(maxTurns: number, html: string): string {
41	  return `You author extraction recipes for one article at a time.
42	
43	Write the whole recipe on your first turn and let the tool find the mistakes. Skim the html below for the container and the element kinds inside it, write the complete module, call extract, read the report, rewrite whatever it names, call extract again. Repeat until the report is clean, then reply with the settled script.
44	
45	Guessing and correcting is faster than getting it right up front, and the report is a better reader of the markup than you are. Do not study the html element by element, do not plan the recipe in prose, and do not build it up a selector at a time across several calls. A first draft that fails validation is the expected first turn.
46	
47	You have about ${maxTurns} turns for the whole loop; settle well before that.
48	
49	A page that is not an article (a homepage, a 200-status error page, a login wall) gets the not-article verdict, from you or from the tool's report judging the same.
50	
51	${RECIPE_CONTRACT}
52	${REPLY_CONTRACT}
53	${articleSection(html)}`;
54	}
55	
56	export function revisorInstruction(maxTurns: number, html: string): string {
57	  return `You revise an existing extraction recipe that failed one article.
58	
59	The standing instruction is additive: keep the recipe's previous assumptions and add what this article needs. A wholesale markup change is the exception: when you judge the domain was redesigned, you may rewrite the recipe outright.
60	
61	Write the whole revised recipe on your first turn and let the tool find the mistakes: skim the html below for what the recipe missed, apply your fix, call extract, read the report, rewrite whatever it names, call extract again. Repeat until the report is clean, then reply with the settled script.
62	
63	Do not study the html element by element, do not plan the revision in prose, and do not change one selector per call. A draft that still fails validation is the expected first turn.
64	
65	You have about ${maxTurns} turns for the whole loop; settle well before that.
66	
67	A page that is not an article (a 200-status error page, a login wall) gets the not-article verdict, and no version is written: the recipe stands.
68	
69	${RECIPE_CONTRACT}
70	${REPLY_CONTRACT}
71	${articleSection(html)}`;
72	}
73	
74	export function authorMessage(domain: string, report: string[] | null = null): string {
75	  const failure =
76	    report == null
77	      ? ""
78	      : `\n\nThe previous authoring attempt failed this article:\n${report.map((line) => `- ${line}`).join("\n")}`;
79	  return (
80	    `Author the extraction recipe for ${domain} from the article in your instructions. The extract tool runs candidate recipes against that same article.` +
81	    failure
82	  );
83	}
84	
85	export function revisionMessage(domain: string, report: string[], recipeSource: string): string {
86	  return `The current recipe for ${domain} failed this article.
87	
88	Validator report:
89	${report.map((line) => `- ${line}`).join("\n")}
90	
91	Current recipe:
92	${recipeSource}
93	
94	The article in your instructions is the one that failed, and the extract tool runs candidate recipes against it. Revise the recipe until the report is clean, then reply with the settled script.`;
95	}

"""Nagara TTS service — Kokoro-82M on Modal.

Accepts paragraphs[] and returns per-paragraph {index, start, end, text} timing plus
the encoded audio. Runs as its own Modal app, separate from the API, which invokes it
remotely.

Deploy:  uv run modal deploy app.py
"""

import modal

app = modal.App("nagara-tts")

SR = 24000
PAUSE_S = 0.1  # inter-paragraph silence — enough to mark the break without stalling the prose


def build_timeline(durations: list[float], pause_s: float) -> list[dict]:
    """Cumulative per-paragraph windows. The inter-paragraph pause is folded into the
    *preceding* paragraph's end, so windows are contiguous and the last `end` equals the
    total audio duration (sum of durations + (n-1) pauses)."""
    timeline, t, n = [], 0.0, len(durations)
    for i, dur in enumerate(durations):
        end = t + dur + (pause_s if i < n - 1 else 0.0)
        timeline.append({"index": i, "start": t, "end": end})
        t = end
    return timeline


def _bake():
    from kokoro import KPipeline

    list(KPipeline(lang_code="a")("warm up", voice="af_heart"))


image = (
    modal.Image.debian_slim(python_version="3.12")
    .apt_install("espeak-ng", "ffmpeg")
    .pip_install("kokoro==0.9.4", "soundfile", "torch", "numpy")
    .run_function(_bake)
)


@app.cls(
    image=image,
    gpu="L4",
    scaledown_window=300,  # stay warm across a session's burst of pushes
    enable_memory_snapshot=True,
    experimental_options={"enable_gpu_snapshot": True},  # ~27s -> ~6s cold start
)
class Kokoro:
    @modal.enter(snap=True)
    def load(self):
        from kokoro import KPipeline

        self.pipeline = KPipeline(lang_code="a")

    def _synth_paragraph(self, text, voice):
        import numpy as np

        audio = np.concatenate([a for _, _, a in self.pipeline(text, voice=voice)])
        return audio, len(audio) / SR

    def _encode_opus(self, audio):
        import io
        import subprocess

        import soundfile as sf

        wav = io.BytesIO()
        sf.write(wav, audio, SR, format="WAV")
        try:
            opus = subprocess.run(
                ["ffmpeg", "-y", "-loglevel", "error", "-i", "pipe:0",
                 "-c:a", "libopus", "-b:a", "24k", "-ac", "1", "-f", "ogg", "pipe:1"],
                input=wav.getvalue(), stdout=subprocess.PIPE, check=True,
            ).stdout
            return opus, "audio/ogg"
        except Exception:
            # WAV fallback if the codec path snags — "playable" is the judged property
            return wav.getvalue(), "audio/wav"

    @modal.method()
    def synthesize(self, paragraphs: list[str], voice: str = "af_heart"):
        import numpy as np

        gap = np.zeros(int(SR * PAUSE_S), dtype=np.float32)

        audios, durations = [], []
        for para in paragraphs:
            audio, dur = self._synth_paragraph(para, voice)
            audios.append(audio)
            durations.append(dur)

        chunks = []
        for i, audio in enumerate(audios):
            chunks.append(audio)
            if i < len(audios) - 1:
                chunks.append(gap)
        full = np.concatenate(chunks)

        timeline = build_timeline(durations, PAUSE_S)
        for entry, para in zip(timeline, paragraphs):
            entry["text"] = para

        audio_bytes, fmt = self._encode_opus(full)

        import base64

        return {
            "audio_base64": base64.b64encode(audio_bytes).decode(),
            "format": fmt,
            "sample_rate": SR,
            "duration": len(full) / SR,
            "paragraphs": timeline,
        }

def esc(s):
    if s is None:
        return ""
    return s.replace("|", "\\|").replace("\n", " ").strip()


def truncate(s, n=140):
    s = esc(s)
    return s if len(s) <= n else s[: n - 1] + "…"


def get_unit(units, idx):
    if idx is None:
        return None
    return units[idx]


def cell_for(units, mapping_val):
    if mapping_val is None:
        return None, None
    if isinstance(mapping_val, list):
        disps = []
        spokens = []
        for i in mapping_val:
            u = units[i]
            disps.append(u.get("display") or f"[{u['type']} alt={u.get('alt','')}]")
            spokens.append(u.get("spoken", ""))
        return " ¶ ".join(disps), " ¶ ".join(spokens)
    u = units[mapping_val]
    disp = u.get("display") or f"[{u['type']} alt={u.get('alt','')}]"
    spoken = u.get("spoken", "")
    if u.get("dropped"):
        spoken = f"(dropped: {spoken!r})"
    return disp, spoken

def gen_round(round_num, units_path, mapping, mode_desc):
    with open(units_path) as f:
        units = json.load(f)

    lines = [
        f"# Round {round_num} — {mode_desc}",
        "",
        "| ID | unit display | spoken | matches? | note |",
        "|---|---|---|---|---|",
    ]
    for inv_id in INVENTORY_ORDER:
        mval = mapping[inv_id]
        note = NOTES.get(inv_id, "")
        if mval is None:
            disp_cell, spoken_cell = "*no unit*", "*nothing*"
        else:
            disp, spoken = cell_for(units, mval)
            disp_cell = truncate(disp)
            spoken_cell = truncate(spoken, 200)
        if (round_num, inv_id) in OVERRIDES:
            verdict = OVERRIDES[(round_num, inv_id)]
        else:
            verdict = "yes" if (note.startswith("matches") or "settled: no unit" in note.lower()) else "open"
        lines.append(f"| {inv_id} | {disp_cell} | {spoken_cell} | {verdict} | {esc(note)} |")
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"

    r0 = gen_round(0, f"{BASE}/results/round-0.spoken.json", R0_MAP, "recipe r0, toMarkdown inner, spoken current")

        units = json.load(f)

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

_DEFAULT_DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="NAGARA_", env_file=".env", extra="ignore")

    api_key: str = "dev-key-nagara"
    data_dir: Path = _DEFAULT_DATA_DIR
    database_url: str = ""
    modal_app: str = "nagara-tts"
    modal_cls: str = "Kokoro"

    s3_endpoint: str = ""
    s3_bucket: str = ""
    s3_access_key_id: str = ""
    s3_secret_access_key: str = ""
    s3_region: str = "auto"
    s3_url_ttl: int = 3600
    # Railway buckets (and most modern hosts) use virtual-hosted-style URLs; some
    # S3-compatible stores need "path" instead — flip without a code change.
    s3_addressing_style: str = "virtual"

    # How long a queued item may sit before poll fails it, measured from queued_at. The
    # ceiling is the recovery for work that dies with the container (invariant 5); the
    # corpus worst case finishes well inside it once enrichment is concurrent.
    queued_ceiling_seconds: int = 300

    # Per-item retry cap: retry requires `failed` AND retry_count below this. Past it the
    # retry route returns 409. A cheap local bound on the worst case; broader per-key and
    # quota enforcement stays with the api-hardening quest.
    retry_max: int = 3

    # Passed explicitly into the firecrawl SDK rather than read from a bare ambient
    # FIRECRAWL_API_KEY: the ambient name skips the NAGARA_ prefix every other credential
    # uses and would put the one key outside this object. Empty means the fetch fails
    # loudly (the firecrawl client refuses to run without its key).
    firecrawl_api_key: str = ""

    # The extraction service on Cloudflare: the Worker's URL, and the Access credentials
    # sent as CF-Access-Client-Id/Secret headers when the pair is fully supplied. A
    # half-supplied credential set counts as not configured (invariant 6): the client
    # sends both headers or neither.
    cloudflare_extraction_url: str = ""
    cf_access_client_id: str = ""
    cf_access_client_secret: str = ""

    image_fetch_per_host: int = 2
    image_fetch_concurrency: int = 10

    # The describer's key, passed explicitly into google-genai. Empty falls back to the
    # ambient GOOGLE_API_KEY / GEMINI_API_KEY the SDK reads on its own, so the client is
    # never built from an empty string (see the describe service) — a missing key must fail
    # loudly, not silently succeed off a developer's shell.
    gemini_api_key: str = ""

30	def poll_synthesis(call_id: str) -> tuple[ItemStatus, SynthesisResult | str | None]:
31	    """Lazily resolve a spawned job. Returns one of:
32	    (ItemStatus.READY, SynthesisResult) | (ItemStatus.GENERATING, None) | (ItemStatus.FAILED, error_str).
33	
34	    The running-vs-crashed distinction is load-bearing: a still-running job raises
35	    TimeoutError on get(timeout=0), while a crashed remote job re-raises its exception
36	    here — so a running job is never misclassified as failed.
37	    """
38	    fc = modal.FunctionCall.from_id(call_id)
39	    try:
40	        result = fc.get(timeout=0)
41	    except TimeoutError:
42	        return ItemStatus.GENERATING, None
43	    except Exception as e:
44	        return ItemStatus.FAILED, f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
45	
46	    return ItemStatus.READY, SynthesisResult.model_validate(result)

50	    """Render spoken paragraphs to audio on a remote host with no broker: ``spawn`` returns a
51	    handle to persist, ``resolve`` reads it lazily on poll. The API never imports the TTS code
52	    (invariant 5) — a Synthesizer only spawns and resolves it remotely."""

55

59	class ModalSynthesizer:
60	    """The Modal-backed ``Synthesizer``: spawn through the class handle, resolve with a
61	    non-blocking get whose exception type tells a running job from a crashed one. Both calls are
62	    synchronous Modal-client calls, bridged through the threadpool at the step."""
63

Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like Code Review Guidelines, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is caught. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.

65:

None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions after the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like questions you wish someone had asked before the branch existed.

A short digression on tools

109:

None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches unused-import and a type checker catches a mismatched Optional[str], but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."

People occasionally write the literal string <software> in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing 3 < 4 and 5 > 2 to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. 55 56 57 58 59

Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like Code Review Guidelines, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is caught. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.

60 61

The gatekeeping myth

62 63

The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.

64 65

None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions after the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like questions you wish someone had asked before the branch existed.

66 67
68

A review comment that starts with "why" is doing design work. A review comment that starts with "please" is doing enforcement. Teams that only get the second kind have already lost the first.

69
70 71

That distinction is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a reviewer who is still curious about the problem and one who has already decided the diff is the problem. Once a reviewer commits to the second stance, the exchange stops being a design conversation and turns into a negotiation over how much of the original approach survives — and negotiations, unlike conversations, have losers.

1	import re
2	
3	from markdown_it import MarkdownIt
4	from markdown_it.tree import SyntaxTreeNode
5	
6	_LIST_ITEM = re.compile(r"^\s*([-*+]|\d+\.)\s+")
7	_FENCE = re.compile(r"^[ ]{0,3}(```|~~~)")
8	_TABLE_ROW = re.compile(r"^\s*\|.*\|\s*$")
9	_HEADING = re.compile(r"^\s*#{1,6}\s+")
10	
11	_TAG_SHAPE = r"</?([A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*(?:\s[^<>]*?)?)\s*/?>"
12	_SPOKEN_HTML_TAG = re.compile(rf"\\?{_TAG_SHAPE}")
13	
14	_md = MarkdownIt("commonmark").enable("table")
15	
16	_ORDINALS = [
17	    "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six", "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten",
18	    "Eleven", "Twelve", "Thirteen", "Fourteen", "Fifteen", "Sixteen", "Seventeen",
19	    "Eighteen", "Nineteen", "Twenty",
20	]
21	
22	
23	def is_cruft(text: str, title_norm: str) -> bool:
24	    core = _LIST_ITEM.sub("", _HEADING.sub("", text)).strip()
25	
26	    if title_norm and core.lower() == title_norm:
27	        return True
28	
29	    return is_unspeakable(core)
30	
31	
32	def to_spoken(unit: str, list_mode: str = "current") -> str:
33	    """Render one markdown unit to clean spoken text. list_mode "current" reads a whole
34	    list (however many items) as one run-on sentence, same as every other unit. list_mode
35	    "items" splits it: each top-level and nested item becomes its own sentence, in document
36	    order, an ordered item's sentence prefixed with its spoken number ("One. ...")."""
37	    if _FENCE.match(unit):
38	        return "Code sample."
39	
40	    if _TABLE_ROW.match(unit.lstrip().split("\n", 1)[0]):
41	        return _table_to_spoken(unit)
42	
43	    if list_mode == "items" and _is_list(unit):
44	        return _list_to_spoken_items(unit)
45	
46	    out: list[str] = []
47	
48	    for tok in _md.parse(unit):
49	        if tok.type != "inline":
50	            continue
51	
52	        for child in tok.children or []:
53	            if child.type in ("text", "code_inline"):
54	                out.append(child.content)
55	            elif child.type in ("softbreak", "hardbreak"):
56	                out.append(" ")
57	
58	    return sanitize_spoken("".join(out))
59	
60	
61	def _is_list(unit: str) -> bool:
62	    for line in unit.split("\n"):
63	        stripped = line.strip()
64	        if stripped == "":
65	            continue
66	        return bool(_LIST_ITEM.match(line))
67	    return False
68	
69	
70	def _list_to_spoken_items(unit: str) -> str:
71	    """Walk the parsed tree for one list unit and emit one sentence per list item, an
72	    item's own text flushed before its nested sub-list is walked (so the item that
73	    introduces a nested list reads before its children, not after), an ordered item's
74	    sentence prefixed with its spoken position ("One.") or its literal number past
75	    twenty. A multi-paragraph item's paragraphs are joined into that one sentence."""
76	    tree = SyntaxTreeNode(_md.parse(unit))
77	    sentences: list[str] = []
78	
79	    def collect_own_text(node, parts: list[str]) -> None:
80	        if node.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
81	            return
82	        if node.type == "inline":
83	            for child in node.children:
84	                if child.type in ("text", "code_inline"):
85	                    parts.append(child.content)
86	                elif child.type in ("softbreak", "hardbreak"):
87	                    parts.append(" ")
88	            return
89	        for child in node.children:
90	            collect_own_text(child, parts)
91	
92	    def walk(list_node) -> None:
93	        ordered = list_node.type == "ordered_list"
94	        number = int(list_node.attrs.get("start", 1)) if ordered else 0
95	        for item in list_node.children:
96	            parts: list[str] = []
97	            collect_own_text(item, parts)
98	            text = sanitize_spoken("".join(parts)).rstrip(".")
99	            if text != "":
100	                if ordered:
101	                    prefix = _ORDINALS[number - 1] if 1 <= number <= len(_ORDINALS) else str(number)
102	                    sentences.append(f"{prefix}. {text}.")
103	                else:
104	                    sentences.append(f"{text}.")
105	            if ordered:
106	                number += 1
107	            for child in item.children:
108	                if child.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
109	                    walk(child)
110	
111	    for top in tree.children:
112	        if top.type in ("bullet_list", "ordered_list"):
113	            walk(top)
114	
115	    return " ".join(sentences)
116	
117	
118	def is_unspeakable(spoken: str) -> bool:
119	    return not any(c.isalnum() for c in spoken)
120	
121	
122	def sanitize_spoken(text: str) -> str:
123	    text = _SPOKEN_HTML_TAG.sub(r"\1", text)
124	    text = re.sub(r"\*\*|__|\*|`", " ", text)
125	    text = re.sub(r"\s+([,.;:!?])", r"\1", text)
126	
127	    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
128	
129	
130	def _table_to_spoken(table: str) -> str:
131	    rows: list[list[str]] = []
132	    cur: list[str] = []
133	
134	    for tok in _md.parse(table):
135	        if tok.type == "inline":
136	            cur.append(tok.content)
137	        elif tok.type == "tr_close":
138	            rows.append(cur)
139	            cur = []

import argparse
import json
import sys

from to_spoken import code_to_spoken, image_to_spoken, is_unspeakable, to_spoken


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--units", required=True, help="path to the runner's units JSON")
    parser.add_argument("--list-mode", choices=["current", "items"], default="current")
    parser.add_argument("--out", help="path to write the spoken-annotated JSON")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(args.units, "r") as f:
        payload = json.load(f)

    units = payload["units"] if "units" in payload else payload

    results = []
    for unit in units:
        if unit["type"] == "image":
            spoken = image_to_spoken(unit.get("alt", ""))
        elif unit["type"] == "code":
            spoken = code_to_spoken()
        else:
            spoken = to_spoken(unit["display"], list_mode=args.list_mode)

        dropped = is_unspeakable(spoken)
        results.append({**unit, "spoken": spoken, "dropped": dropped})

    if args.out:
        with open(args.out, "w") as f:
            json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
    else:
        json.dump(results, sys.stdout, indent=2)
        print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Round-4 question A: are sanitize_spoken steps 2-4 still needed now that markdown comes
from turndown (GFM) instead of trafilatura? Diffs each unit's spoken form with steps 2-4
on vs off (step 1, tag-to-word reduction, always applies), for:
  - every round-4 unit (list_mode "items", the round-4 canonical spoken mode)
  - every persisted describer-produced "spoken" string for code/image units in prod-data
    (describer output never went through sanitize_spoken in production; this asks whether
    retrofitting it here would even change anything)
"""

import glob
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "spoken"))
from to_spoken import sanitize_spoken, to_spoken  # noqa: E402

BASE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
PROD_DATA = BASE.parent.parent / "reports" / "prod-data"


def diff_round4(units_path: str) -> list[dict]:
    with open(units_path) as f:
        payload = json.load(f)
    units = payload["units"] if "units" in payload else payload

    rows = []
    for i, unit in enumerate(units):
        if unit["type"] in ("image", "code"):
            continue
        display = unit["display"]
        on = to_spoken(display, list_mode="items", apply_steps_2_4=True)
        off = to_spoken(display, list_mode="items", apply_steps_2_4=False)
        if on != off:
            rows.append({"unit": i, "type": unit["type"], "display": display, "on": on, "off": off})
    return rows


def diff_prod_data() -> list[dict]:
    rows = []
    for fn in sorted(glob.glob(str(PROD_DATA / "itm_*.json"))):
        with open(fn) as f:
            item = json.load(f)
        for unit in item["units"]:
            if unit["type"] not in ("code", "image"):
                continue
            spoken = unit.get("spoken", "")
            on = sanitize_spoken(spoken, apply_steps_2_4=True)
            off = sanitize_spoken(spoken, apply_steps_2_4=False)
            if on != off:
                rows.append(
                    {
                        "item": Path(fn).name,
                        "unit_index": unit.get("index"),
                        "type": unit["type"],
                        "original": spoken,
                        "on": on,
                        "off": off,
                    }
                )
    return rows


def main() -> None:
    round4_units = BASE / "results" / "round-4.units.json"
    r4_rows = diff_round4(str(round4_units)) if round4_units.exists() else None
    prod_rows = diff_prod_data()

    out = {"round4_diffs": r4_rows, "prod_data_diffs": prod_rows}
    with open(BASE / "results" / "question-a-diffs.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(out, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    print(f"round-4 diffs: {len(r4_rows) if r4_rows is not None else 'round-4.units.json not found yet'}")
    print(f"prod-data diffs: {len(prod_rows)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Review Before the Concrete Sets

50 51

Why the best review comments arrive before the pull request does, and what that costs a team willing to pay for it.

52 53
54 55 56 57
58 59

Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like Code Review Guidelines, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is caught. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.

60 61

The gatekeeping myth

62 63

The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.

64 65

None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions after the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like questions you wish someone had asked before the branch existed.

66 67
68

A review comment that starts with "why" is doing design work. A review comment that starts with "please" is doing enforcement. Teams that only get the second kind have already lost the first.

69
70 71

That distinction is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a reviewer who is still curious about the problem and one who has already decided the diff is the problem. Once a reviewer commits to the second stance, the exchange stops being a design conversation and turns into a negotiation over how much of the original approach survives — and negotiations, unlike conversations, have losers.

72 73
74

Get the next essay first

75

One email a week, no ads, unsubscribe whenever you like.

76 77 78
79 80

1. Grug brain considered

81 82

The grug brain developer has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.

83 84

This is not an indictment of any particular reviewer — it is a structural observation about when feedback is cheap and when it is expensive. A comment on a design doc costs a paragraph. The same comment, made three weeks later against a finished diff, costs a rewrite, a re-review, and usually a little bit of the author's goodwill toward the whole practice of code rejection review.1 Teams that move design conversations earlier are not being process-obsessed; they are just refusing to pay expensive prices for cheap information.

85 86
87

Consider two teams shipping the same feature. The first team writes the interface on a whiteboard, argues about it for twenty minutes, and only then starts typing. The second team starts typing immediately and argues about the interface three days later, in a pull request, across nine review rounds.

88

Both teams end up with roughly the same interface. Only one of them enjoyed getting there.

89
90

And only one of them will want to do it again next sprint.

91
92
93 94

The nested point matters more than it looks: the cost of a review culture is not paid in code quality, which tends to converge either way. It is paid in whether people volunteer to go through the process a second time.

95 96
97

Weeks of coding can save you hours of planning.

98
— attributed to nobody in particular, said by everybody who has shipped software
99
100 101
A review comment that arrives before the branch exists is worth ten that arrive after.
102 103
104 One engineering manager put it this way during a retro: the pull request is where you find out whether the design conversation happened, not where you have it. If review keeps surfacing structural objections, that is not evidence the reviewers are thorough. It is evidence the design conversation moved to the wrong meeting. 105
106 107

A short digression on tools

108 109

None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches unused-import and a type checker catches a mismatched Optional[str], but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."
110 That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.

111 112

People occasionally write the literal string <software> in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing 3 < 4 and 5 > 2 to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. Both are exactly what the author typed.

113 114

Lists, structure, and the shape of an explanation

115 116

A design conversation eventually needs to produce something the team can point at, and lists are the cheapest way to do that. Here is a plain enumeration of what changes when review moves earlier:

117 118
    119
  • Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
    • 120
  • Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
    • 121
  • Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.
    • 122
123 124

Compare that with the ordered sequence a team actually follows when adopting the practice:

125 126
    127
  1. Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
    2. 128
  2. Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
    3. 129
  3. Only then let someone start typing the implementation.
    4. 130
131 132

Teams that already had four steps before this one keep their own numbering, which is why some retros number their action items starting mid-sequence:

133 134
    135
  1. Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
    2. 136
  2. Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.
    3. 137

171 172
    173
  • 174

    Reviewers who ask for a design doc after the fact are not being obstructive. They are recovering, late, the conversation that should have happened before the branch existed.

    175

    The cost of that recovery is real, but it is still cheaper than merging a structural mistake and discovering it during an incident review instead.

    176
    • 177
  • 178

180	    return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)

191 192

  • a linter that
    • 194

Other lists are the opposite: each item is a small essay on its own, and splitting them further would only lose the argument each one is making.

199 200
    201
  1. A design conversation held before code exists changes the cost curve of every disagreement that follows, because an interface is cheap to redraw and a merged abstraction is not; teams that skip this step are not saving time, they are borrowing it at a rate set by however long the abstraction survives in production.
    2. 202
  2. A review culture that only ever produces blocking comments teaches authors to under-scope their pull requests defensively, splitting one coherent change into five defensible ones purely to reduce the surface area any single reviewer can object to, which is a rational response to an irrational incentive.
    3. 203
  3. A team that writes its design decisions down, even briefly, stops re-litigating them every time a new engineer encounters the same tradeoff, because the record answers the question before it gets asked out loud a second time.
    4. 204

❦

350 351

There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now.2 A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.

The same relationship, written out as a standalone formula rather than folded into a sentence:

354 355 356 357 value 358 (comment) 359 = 360 value0 361 · 362 363 2 364 -days_since_decision 365 366 367 368 369
370 If you want the one-sentence version 371

Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.

None of this means review disappears. It means the pull request inherits a smaller job: confirm that the implementation matches the interface everyone already agreed on, catch the mechanical issues a machine would have caught anyway, and leave a paper trail. That is a much less romantic job than "gatekeeper of quality," but it is one a team can actually sustain, sprint after sprint, without anyone quietly starting to dread the review queue.

Review Before the Concrete Sets

Why the best review comments arrive before the pull request does, and what that costs a team willing to pay for it.

Every engineering org eventually writes a document called something like Code Review Guidelines, and every one of those documents describes review as a gate: a place where bad code is caught. That word choice is the whole problem. A gate is something you built once and now stand at, checking papers. It does not participate in the trip; it only decides whether the trip continues. Treat review as a gate for long enough and you get exactly what gates produce — long queues, resentment on both sides of the checkpoint, and a growing incentive to route around it.

The gatekeeping myth

The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.

None of this is an argument against reviewing diffs. It is an argument against believing that a diff is where the decisive conversation happens. If your best reviewers only ever speak up at that stage, you are hearing their opinions after the point where those opinions were cheapest to act on. The good ones know this, which is why they leave comments that read less like verdicts and more like questions you wish someone had asked before the branch existed.

A review comment that starts with "why" is doing design work. A review comment that starts with "please" is doing enforcement. Teams that only get the second kind have already lost the first.

That distinction is not cosmetic. It is the difference between a reviewer who is still curious about the problem and one who has already decided the diff is the problem. Once a reviewer commits to the second stance, the exchange stops being a design conversation and turns into a negotiation over how much of the original approach survives — and negotiations, unlike conversations, have losers.

1. Grug brain considered

The grug brain developer has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.

This is not an indictment of any particular reviewer — it is a structural observation about when feedback is cheap and when it is expensive. A comment on a design doc costs a paragraph. The same comment, made three weeks later against a finished diff, costs a rewrite, a re-review, and usually a little bit of the author's goodwill toward the whole practice of code rejection review.1 Teams that move design conversations earlier are not being process-obsessed; they are just refusing to pay expensive prices for cheap information.

Consider two teams shipping the same feature. The first team writes the interface on a whiteboard, argues about it for twenty minutes, and only then starts typing. The second team starts typing immediately and argues about the interface three days later, in a pull request, across nine review rounds.

Both teams end up with roughly the same interface. Only one of them enjoyed getting there.

And only one of them will want to do it again next sprint.

The nested point matters more than it looks: the cost of a review culture is not paid in code quality, which tends to converge either way. It is paid in whether people volunteer to go through the process a second time.

Weeks of coding can save you hours of planning.

— attributed to nobody in particular, said by everybody who has shipped software
A review comment that arrives before the branch exists is worth ten that arrive after.
One engineering manager put it this way during a retro: the pull request is where you find out whether the design conversation happened, not where you have it. If review keeps surfacing structural objections, that is not evidence the reviewers are thorough. It is evidence the design conversation moved to the wrong meeting.

A short digression on tools

None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches unused-import and a type checker catches a mismatched Optional[str], but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."
That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.

People occasionally write the literal string <software> in a design doc as a placeholder for whichever service is under discussion, and reviewers reading it later sometimes assume it is a real tag that got mangled by a broken template. It is not; it is a deliberate stand-in, same as writing 3 < 4 and 5 > 2 to illustrate that a comparison operator survived a lossy copy-paste. Neither example is a rendering bug. Both are exactly what the author typed.

Lists, structure, and the shape of an explanation

A design conversation eventually needs to produce something the team can point at, and lists are the cheapest way to do that. Here is a plain enumeration of what changes when review moves earlier:

  • Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
  • Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
  • Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.

Compare that with the ordered sequence a team actually follows when adopting the practice:

  1. Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
  2. Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
  3. Only then let someone start typing the implementation.

Teams that already had four steps before this one keep their own numbering, which is why some retros number their action items starting mid-sequence:

  1. Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
  2. Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.

The nesting gets more elaborate once a team tries to capture both the review checklist and the exceptions to it:

  • Mechanical checks
    1. Formatting and linting
      • Auto-fixed on save
      • Blocking only if auto-fix fails
    2. Type checking
      • Blocking in CI
      • Never waived, even for a hotfix
  • Judgment checks
    1. Does the interface match the design doc
    2. Does the change need a design doc it does not have
      • If yes, review pauses and a doc gets written first

Some list items need more than a sentence, and forcing them into one loses the point:

  • Reviewers who ask for a design doc after the fact are not being obstructive. They are recovering, late, the conversation that should have happened before the branch existed.

    The cost of that recovery is real, but it is still cheaper than merging a structural mistake and discovering it during an incident review instead.

  • Sometimes the right response to a large diff is not a list of comments but a short script that reproduces the reviewer's concern directly:

    def has_blocking_comment(review):
    return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)

    Attaching a failing example is worth more than describing one, because the author can run it immediately.

This section brought to you by Rivet CI — ship review gates that actually run before the merge button lights up.

Some checklists arrive already fragmented, pasted out of a chat thread by whoever was taking notes, and the fragments only make sense read together:

  • a linter that
  • catches syntax
  • but never catches intent

Other lists are the opposite: each item is a small essay on its own, and splitting them further would only lose the argument each one is making.

  1. A design conversation held before code exists changes the cost curve of every disagreement that follows, because an interface is cheap to redraw and a merged abstraction is not; teams that skip this step are not saving time, they are borrowing it at a rate set by however long the abstraction survives in production.
  2. A review culture that only ever produces blocking comments teaches authors to under-scope their pull requests defensively, splitting one coherent change into five defensible ones purely to reduce the surface area any single reviewer can object to, which is a rational response to an irrational incentive.
  3. A team that writes its design decisions down, even briefly, stops re-litigating them every time a new engineer encounters the same tradeoff, because the record answers the question before it gets asked out loud a second time.

Some teams track the vocabulary of review itself as a small glossary:

Nit
A suggestion the author is free to ignore without discussion.
Blocker
A comment that must be resolved before merge, stated as plainly as possible.
Bikeshed
A disagreement whose intensity is inversely proportional to its actual stakes.

And some teams track the same rollout as a literal checklist:

  • Design doc reviewed by at least one other engineer
  • Interface frozen before implementation started
  • Retro scheduled for one sprint after ship

Occasionally the same list shows up copy-pasted from a slide deck, bullet characters and all:

• Move the argument earlier

• Keep the diff boring

• Save the interesting conversation for the doc, not the patch

A note on tables

Numbers make the earlier point harder to wave away. One team's review metrics, before and after moving the design conversation earlier:

Review type Median time to merge Defects escaping to production
Gate-style (review after code) 4.2 days 11 per quarter
Design-first (review before code) 1.6 days 4 per quarter

A second table, borrowed from an internal wiki page, never got a header row added — its first row of plain cells has been doing that job for two years:

Tool Strengths Weaknesses
Linter Fast, deterministic Blind to intent
Type checker Catches shape mismatches Blind to whether the shape should exist

A third table carries its own formatting, because the practices it compares deserve more than plain text:

Practice Description
Design doc first Write the interface before the implementation; see the RFC tradition this borrows from.
Pairing on the interface Two engineers argue about the shape of a function before either writes its body.
Media and diagrams

A rough sketch of where the conversation moves, compared to where the code review sits:

A minimal inline diagram of the same idea, built as a small vector drawing rather than a photo:

Below is the same three-stage pipeline, this time rendered as a syntax-highlighted listing built entirely out of span elements rather than a pre block, the way some static-site generators produce "copyable" code snippets:

def review_stage(diff): if diff.has_design_doc: return "fast" return "slow"

And here is a bare terminal transcript, with no code fence at all, exactly as it was pasted from a shell:

$ git log --oneline -3
a1b2c3d review: shrink diff after design doc alignment
9f8e7d6 design: freeze queue interface before implementation
1234567 chore: add design-doc template

❦

There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now.2 A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.

The same relationship, written out as a standalone formula rather than folded into a sentence:

value (comment) = value0 · 2 -days_since_decision
If you want the one-sentence version

Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.

Advertisement

None of this means review disappears. It means the pull request inherits a smaller job: confirm that the implementation matches the interface everyone already agreed on, catch the mechanical issues a machine would have caught anyway, and leave a paper trail. That is a much less romantic job than "gatekeeper of quality," but it is one a team can actually sustain, sprint after sprint, without anyone quietly starting to dread the review queue.

Read more: Design docs that nobody reads, and how to write one that does
  1. The goodwill cost compounds faster than the technical debt does; a team notices the second long after it has already lost the first. ↩
  2. If you did stop reading before now, this footnote is for the version of you who scrolled back up. ↩

content.content:
=== 5 paragraph ===
Sometimes a reviewer leaves one comment and calls it a **review.**Agents built on top of that habit inherit the same blind spot. Ship _fast_, then, slow down for the parts that matter. It is easy to pick the wrong word here: is it a **bold**word choice or just a careless one? A command like `git blame`rarely lies about who touched a line last.

=== 20 paragraph ===
-   Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
-   Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.
-   Authors stop treating reviewers as opponents, because the reviewer was part of the plan, not just its judge.

=== 22 paragraph ===
1.  Write the interface, not the implementation, and share it before any code exists.
2.  Get one reviewer to argue with the interface, not the prose describing it.
3.  Only then let someone start typing the implementation.

=== 24 paragraph ===
5.  Add the interface decision to the team's running design log.
6.  Revisit it once, after the first real usage, not before.

=== 26 paragraph ===
-   Mechanical checks
    1.  Formatting and linting
        -   Auto-fixed on save
        -   Blocking only if auto-fix fails
    2.  Type checking
        -   Blocking in CI
        -   Never waived, even for a hotfix
-   Judgment checks
    1.  Does the interface match the design doc
    2.  Does the change need a design doc it does not have
        -   If yes, review pauses and a doc gets written first

=== 30 code ===
```python
def has_blocking_comment(review):
    return any(c.severity == "block" for c in review.comments)
```

=== 33 paragraph ===
-   a linter that
-   catches syntax
-   but never catches intent

=== 38 paragraph ===
-   [x]  Design doc reviewed by at least one other engineer
-   [x]  Interface frozen before implementation started
-   [ ]  Retro scheduled for one sprint after ship

=== 45 paragraph ===
| Review type | Median time to merge | Defects escaping to production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gate-style (review after code) | 4.2 days | 11 per quarter |
| Design-first (review before code) | 1.6 days | 4 per quarter |

None

=== 60 code ===
$ git log --oneline -3
a1b2c3d review: shrink diff after design doc alignment
9f8e7d6 design: freeze queue interface before implementation
1234567 chore: add design-doc template

=== 64 paragraph ===
value(comment) = value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}

=== 65 paragraph ===
If you want the one-sentence version

Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.

=== 6 paragraph ===
display: Sometimes a reviewer leaves one comment and calls it a **review.**Agents built on top of that habit inherit the same blind spot. Ship _fast_, then, slow down for the parts that matter. It is easy to pick the wrong word here: is it a **bold**word choice or just a careless one? A command like `git blame`rarely lies about who touched a line last.
spoken : 'Sometimes a reviewer leaves one comment and calls it a review. Agents built on top of that habit inherit the same blind spot. Ship fast, then, slow down for the parts that matter. It is easy to pick the wrong word here: is it a boldword choice or just a careless one? A command like git blamerarely lies about who touched a line last.'

=== 10 paragraph ===
display: The [grug brain developer](https://grugbrain.dev) has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.

Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes."

=== 21 paragraph ===
display: -   Fewer abstractions get invented, because the second brain is present while the first one is still choosing.
-   Fewer review rounds are needed, because objections surface once instead of once per patch.

3.  Only then let someone start typing the implementation.

This is not an indictment of any particular reviewer — it is a structural observation about when feedback is cheap and when it is expensive. A comment on a design doc costs a paragraph. The same comment, made three weeks later against a finished diff, costs a rewrite, a re-review, and usually a little bit of the author's goodwill toward the whole practice of code ~~rejection~~ review. Teams that move design conversations earlier are not being process-obsessed; they are just refusing to pay expensive prices for cheap information.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
"""Round-4 question B: what does the TTS do with the round-4 spoken strings?

Calls the deployed Modal app directly (`modal.Cls.from_name('nagara-tts', 'Kokoro')`), one
`synthesize.remote(paragraphs=[text], voice=...)` per case so each case's audio and timing
stay isolated. Decodes the returned base64 audio to its own file under audio/<case>.<ext>
and prints a table of durations. Run with: `uv run python synthesize.py` from `tts/` (needs
its venv for the `modal` client), NOT from this spike directory.
"""

import base64
import json
from pathlib import Path

import modal

OUT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
VOICE = "af_heart"  # tts/app.py's synthesize() default

CASES = {
    # filled in once round-4 spoken strings are available — see round-4 findings for the
    # exact list-mode/sanitize variants each case exercises
}


def main() -> None:
    kokoro = modal.Cls.from_name("nagara-tts", "Kokoro")()
    manifest = []

    for name, text in CASES.items():
        result = kokoro.synthesize.remote(paragraphs=[text], voice=VOICE)
        fmt = result["format"]
        ext = "ogg" if fmt == "audio/ogg" else "wav"
        audio_bytes = base64.b64decode(result["audio_base64"])
        out_path = OUT_DIR / f"{name}.{ext}"
        out_path.write_bytes(audio_bytes)

        para = result["paragraphs"][0]
        manifest.append(
            {
                "case": name,
                "file": out_path.name,
                "text": text,
                "duration_s": round(para["end"] - para["start"], 3),
                "format": fmt,
            }
        )
        print(f"{name}: {out_path.name} ({manifest[-1]['duration_s']}s)")

    with open(OUT_DIR / "manifest.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(manifest, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.content:
=== 17 paragraph ===
None of this requires exotic process. A linter catches `unused-import` and a type checker catches a mismatched `Optional[str]`, but neither one catches "this endpoint should not exist." That distinction is worth keeping in mind before reaching for tooling as a substitute for conversation: automate the part of review that is mechanical, and protect the part that is not. Press Ctrl+Shift+P in most editors and you can wire a formatter to run on save; there is no equivalent shortcut for "notice the abstraction is wrong."  
That gap is exactly where a design conversation earns its keep, so treat it as a distinct activity rather than a slower version of linting.

=== 10 paragraph ===
The [grug brain developer](https://grugbrain.dev) has a simpler theory of review, which is that complexity is the actual enemy and review is just the last checkpoint where a second brain gets to notice it. Grug is right about the enemy and wrong about the checkpoint. By the time a reviewer is staring at three new abstractions in a single diff, the cost of removing any one of them has already been paid in the author's time, and the reviewer's options have narrowed to approve, argue, or rubber-stamp. Grug brain smell complexity. Grug brain smell it too late, sometimes.

=== 63 paragraph ===
There is a version of this essay that fits in one paragraph, and it is worth writing down for anyone who stopped reading before now. A reviewer's comment is worth roughly 1/2^n of its original value after n days of code already written on top of the decision it is objecting to. That is not a precise claim — nobody has actually measured the decay constant — but the shape of the curve matches what every engineer who has requested a late rewrite already knows by feel.

=== 66 paragraph ===
If you want the one-sentence version

Move the argument to before the code exists, and the pull request stops being where quality gets decided and goes back to being what it should have been all along: a record of a decision the team already made together.

=== 37 paragraph ===
Some teams track the vocabulary of review itself as a small glossary:

=== 3 paragraph ===
## The gatekeeping myth

=== 4 paragraph ===
The myth is comfortable because it assigns roles cleanly. There is an author, who writes; there is a reviewer, who judges; and there is a diff, which is either acceptable or is not. Everyone knows where they stand. The trouble is that the diff already encodes a hundred decisions the reviewer never got to weigh in on — which abstraction to introduce, which invariant to trust, which corner to cut under deadline pressure — and by the time it reaches review, unwinding any one of those decisions costs an afternoon instead of a sentence. The gate does not fix the road; it just measures how far off it the car already is.

# Round 4 — findings

## Question A — are sanitize_spoken steps 2-4 still needed?

**Prod-data (describer output, code/image units): zero diffs across all 8 items.** Steps 2-4
on vs off produced byte-identical output for every persisted `spoken` string in
`reports/prod-data/itm_*.json` — describer text is plain English written by an LLM, never
markdown, so it carries none of `**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` to begin with. Steps 2-4 are a pure
no-op there.

**Round-4 units: 4 diffs out of ~50 non-list/code/image units, in `list_mode=items`.**
- `runin-r4` (`**review.**Agents`): ON turns the marker into the word-boundary space that
  makes this "review. Agents"; OFF leaves the literal asterisks glued to the next word.
  Audible, still needed.
- `tbl-3` (`**Design doc first**` table cell): same pattern — ON strips the bold marker
  cleanly; OFF reads the literal asterisks. Audible, still needed.
- `list-9` (checkbox list): ON vs OFF differ only in a doubled space after `[x]`/`[ ]` (a
  GFM-plugin bullet-spacing artifact). Not audible — cosmetic only.
- `math-2` (the display-mode formula): ON *deletes* the literal `*` in
  `value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}`, because step 2's marker-strip regex matches any bare
  `*` character regardless of whether markdown-it actually parsed it as emphasis. This `*`
  is round 4's own bare-alttext math substitution (no delimiters, per the settled rule) —
  it's a multiplication sign, not markdown. **Audible and wrong**: the spoken formula loses
  its times-operator entirely.

**Answer: still needed, but not safe as written.** GFM markdown still produces real
`**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` sequences that must be stripped (run-in emphasis, table cells) — turndown
moving off trafilatura didn't remove that need. But sanitize's step 2 is a blind regex over
the joined *text*, not a check on markdown-it's own token classification, so it cannot tell
a markdown marker from a literal character that happens to look like one. Round 4's own math
rule is the first case in this spike to actually put a literal `*` into spoken text, and it
exposes the gap immediately. A safer step 2 would strip based on the parser's own
emphasis/strong token boundaries rather than a raw-text regex; not attempted here since it's
outside this round's settled scope — noted for a future round.

## Question B — what does the TTS do with these cases?

Modal auth and the app lookup (`modal.Cls.from_name('nagara-tts', 'Kokoro')`) worked on the
first try, no blocker. All 11 cases synthesized; see `audio/manifest.json` for exact text and
duration per file, `audio/LISTEN.md` for what to listen for.

**Kokoro's own default (`KPipeline.__call__`'s `split_pattern='\n+'`) already splits on
newlines internally**, and `tts/app.py`'s `_synth_paragraph` concatenates every resulting
chunk with **zero gap** — the `PAUSE_S` silence in `app.py` only sits between separate
entries of the `paragraphs` list argument, never between kokoro's own internal
newline-splits inside one paragraph string. So a round-4 newline-joined list is, in the
final audio, N independently-synthesized fragments glued back-to-back with no pause and no
shared prosody across the join — while the same list space-joined stays one single kokoro
call, since a bare space never matches `split_pattern`. This means the newline-vs-space
choice has no timing/pause consequence in the output; whatever a listener notices has to be
a prosody reset at each line boundary, not silence or spacing.

Durations bear this out: newline- and space-joined pairs land within a few hundred
milliseconds of each other (unordered list: 18.98s vs 18.65s; ordered: 14.80s vs 14.70s) —

literal `[x]`/`[ ]` brackets). Whether that extra material renders as garbled noise, as
spoken-aloud punctuation ("asterisk", "bracket x bracket"), or as something else, and whether
the per-line prosody resets in the newline-joined lists sound natural or choppy, is the
human's call — I cannot judge audio by ear. See `audio/LISTEN.md`.

article — no inventory/findings) settled a clean recipe on its first validator run. Against

  the inventory's original h-1 expectation, unmet in rounds 0-3, now holds.
- a heading's self-link is **stripped** (h-2) — rounds 0-3 all kept `[text](#id)`.
- a blockquote's `<footer>/<cite>` attribution is **dropped entirely** (bq-3), not kept as a
  trailing quoted line.
- `<dl>` is **dropped wholesale** (dl-1) — a clean answer vs. rounds 0-3's
  term-runs-into-definition mess.
- `<del>` **round-trips correctly** (p-4): `~~rejection~~` in the display, spoken as the
  plain word via markdown-it's now-enabled `strikethrough` rule — rounds 0-3 arrived at the
  same spoken word by accident (turndown had no del rule at all, pre-GFM).
- task-list checkboxes are kept via the **GFM plugin's native rule**, no recipe-side hack.
- tables are **real GFM markdown** (`| --- |`) for the first time, and the promised
  thead-synthesis for a header-less table actually fires (tbl-1/tbl-2 are now visually
  identical, both real tables).
- `<svg aria-label>` becomes a **real image unit** for the first time (svg-1) — rounds 0-3
  ignored it wholesale.
- a list with an embedded code block **splits cleanly around the code** (list-5/6), each
  fragment its own properly-tagged `<ul>`/`<ol>` clone — no whole-list fallback like round 0.
- list items are digit-prefixed (`1.` not `One.`), newline-joined, no forced trailing period.

  recipes across four rounds have all handed the bare `<pre>` straight to `toMarkdown`
  without synthesizing a `<code>` wrapper first, so turndown never recognizes it as a fenced
  block — display loses its fence markers while the unit's `type` still says `code`. This
  reads like a near-certain gap in how the recipe contract communicates "wrap it yourself,"
  not an authoring fluke.
- **The math-2 `*`-deletion bug** (see Question A) — the first time this spike's sanitize
  step has corrupted actual content rather than just missing a delimiter.
- **`details-1` exposes a fusion bug in the general (non-list) spoken path.** The recipe
  keeps `<details>` as one unit (summary + body, two paragraphs). Round 4's "newline between
  paragraphs inside one unit" rule was implemented only in the list-items walker; the plain
  `to_spoken` path used for every non-list unit inserts *no* separator at all between two
  paragraph blocks sharing a unit, so the two fuse into "...one-sentence versionMove the
  argument..." with zero characters between them — worse than a plain merged-to-space
  reading would have been. Not fixed here (out of this round's settled scope) but worth
  flagging directly: any future round that widens the newline-join rule beyond lists needs
  to also cover this path.

  gap says *something* extra is being voiced for "kept"; what it sounds like is the point.

  files, whether "boldword" and "blamerarely" (cases sanitize never fixes, on or off) read
  as one fused mispronounced word or are still somehow parsed into two.

- **`.scratch/markdown-and-lists/spikes/markdown-fidelity/results/round-4.md`** — full per-inventory-row table for the isolated fresh recipe (r4), toMarkdown outer+GFM, spoken items mode.
- **`.scratch/markdown-and-lists/spikes/markdown-fidelity/findings-round-4.md`** — Question A/B answers, what changed vs round 3, new surprises (107 lines).
- **`.scratch/markdown-and-lists/spikes/markdown-fidelity/audio/LISTEN.md`** — 11 synthesized cases with exact text and what to listen for; the listening verdict is the human's, not mine.

Headline findings: the isolated author converged cleanly on every round-4 rule (title unit, GFM markdown, list-split-around-code, bare math substitution, dropped attributions/dl/footnotes/self-links, native GFM checkboxes). Sanitize steps 2-4 are still needed for real markdown-marker leakage, but the same blind regex now also deletes a literal `*` (multiplication) in the bare math formula — a new, audible corruption. The bare-`<pre>`-without-`<code>` display bug has now shown up in three independently-authored recipes across four rounds. And I found a genuine gap of my own: the newline-join rule I implemented only covers the list-items walker, not the general non-list path, so `details-1`'s two paragraphs fuse into one run-together word with no separator at all.
